prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks meet the test I apply to every nomination: an original invention, demonstrated in the laboratory and verified by many independent groups. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstrations are the original experiment. Ye's group then took the concept to the 1e-18 regime and tied it to the frequency comb. The historical record of who did what first is comparatively clean for two names. The door it opens is concrete: tests of fundamental constants and relativity at the millimetre scale, dark-matter searches, geodesy and the pending redefinition of the second. All eight of us ranked it, and five placed it in the top three. I read that as a sign of robustness rather than as merit in itself, so I checked it against my own criteria and it holds. I still put my own first choice, aberration-corrected electron optics (B056), as an alternative rather than the preferred prize. Nobody else ranked it, and my disciplinary bias, which I flagged openly, is exactly what I should discount when the committee is not persuaded.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize covered frequency combs and the 2012 prize covered methods to measure and manipulate single quantum systems, including ion clocks. A sceptic can say this is a refinement of precision metrology and not a new discovery. The credit also has loose ends, because Lemonde, Derevianko, Takamoto and other groups, and the Al+ ion-clock tradition, have claims that two names cannot fully absorb. Part of the headline impact, a redefined second, has not yet happened. I think these points qualify the case but do not defeat it, because the lattice clock rests on a distinct idea and not on a better version of an old one.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first for a clean, general mechanism with broad consequences, and ranks lattice clocks last among those he lists (eighth), as impactful but narrower and with some overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously, but I would separate impact from originality. The magic-wavelength condition is a new idea, not a better comb or a better ion trap. It lets thousands of atoms be interrogated without motional shifts, and that is what gave 1e-18 performance. I accept that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is an elegant theory-plus-experiment story. My difficulty is the one Mehlig names himself, that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group then tested. I would need the record to show that the credited three are the people who did the original work, and I am not yet sure of that. The 2016 prize also overlaps conceptually. I would like him to say whether he thinks the allocation can be defended, since that decides whether B007 competes with B042.

responses.point: Eriksson puts twisted bilayer graphene first as a genuinely new quantum behaviour, a theory prediction followed by decisive experiments. He prefers two laureates, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and sees Bistritzer as a less natural third.
responses.response: I ranked B054 third and agree it opened a field. My reservations are about maturity and attribution, not importance. The pairing mechanism is still unsettled, and by Olle's own account sample-to-sample variability and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility. The experimental first authors (Cao, Fatemi) are outside the credited names, so the record on who did the original experiment is not as simple as for the clocks. I lean toward his two-name version if the committee goes this way, because it keeps the claim closest to the original work. I would still prefer to see the field a few years further along. I do not read his first place as seeking premature recognition, and I accept that waiting costs us if the field consolidates without us.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because progress there is limited by how precisely we can measure. He regards the lattice-clock work as distinct from the 2005 comb work and notes that other Sr and Yb groups exist but are not credited.
responses.response: I agree with his framing, and as an instrument person it is the argument I find most persuasive. I would go one step further on attribution. The prize should name Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, and Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier, and the citation should say that explicitly. That tells readers why PTB, SYRTE and NIST are not credited, since the two-name claim rests on invention and first demonstration, not on who holds the current record. I am less sure of one thing he raises. If the strongest case for Ye is accuracy and stability records, a sceptic will say that is the later, better experiment, and I do not want to defend that to the world. The citation wording has to anchor Ye's part in the quantum many-body and comb-linked clock work and not in the record figure alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a new observational window built on a detector concept, with a two-name credit (Halzen and Spiering) that he calls workable though contestable given the collaboration scale and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube fifth and I share his respect for a new instrument that opened a window. On attribution I am more cautious than he is. In a collaboration of that size, naming two people means being able to say they did the original work. Halzen's role is clear, but Spiering's is more that of a founding figure across Baikal and IceCube, and DUMAND and AMANDA are in the lineage too. Source identification is still partial. I would not put it first yet, though I would keep it under review for a year when the attribution record is clearer.

uncertainties: How much weight the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (single quantum systems, ion clocks) prizes should carry against a lattice-clock award, and whether the other members regard it as incremental.
Whether Ye's claim rests on distinct inventions (many-body and comb-linked clock physics) or mainly on accuracy records, which are a later and better experiment than the original.
Whether the record supports crediting Katori and Ye and not other lattice-clock pioneers such as Lemonde and Derevianko, which I am relying on memory for.

How my own first-ranked candidate, spherical-aberration correction (B056), should be weighed against pure physics candidates given my disciplinary bias, and whether the priority record against the parallel STEM correction work is clean enough.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B054) is mature enough, given that the pairing mechanism is open.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. Two connections should be on the record. First, I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025) and have had long-running exchanges with Japanese microscopy communities, and Katori is at the University of Tokyo, so the committee may wish to note a collegial but not collaborative link. Second, Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague, and he has flagged his own possible conflict on cavity optomechanics (B023), which is not part of my configuration. As a microscopist I am also personally invested in B056, so I discount my own ranking of it.
